report:
Your “no” is too absolute. The better answer is: **olive leaf extract may modestly lower blood pressure in people with borderline or stage‑1 hypertension, but the evidence is small, short-term, and not strong enough to treat it as a proven antihypertensive or replacement for medication.**

A double-blind randomized active-controlled trial reported that 500 mg twice daily reduced systolic/diastolic BP in stage‑1 hypertension and performed comparably to captopril over 8 weeks, but it was small and used a specific extract (https://scholar.ui.ac.id/en/publications/olive-olea-europaea-leaf-extract-effective-in-patients-with-stage/). An earlier co-twin study in borderline hypertensive monozygotic twins also found BP reductions with 500–1000 mg/day, but involved only 40 people and was linked to a supplement ingredient (https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2008/08/27/Olive-leaf-extract-shows-heart-benefits-Frutarom-study/). A later systematic review/meta-analysis suggests an effect, yet the retrieved summary notes included low-quality studies and heterogeneous products/doses (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/361409918_The_effect_of_olive_leaf_use_on_blood_pressure_A_systematic_review_and_meta-analysis). Independent evidence summaries remain cautious: human hypertension data are limited, mechanisms are unclear, and at least one animal study found no BP effect (https://examine.com/supplements/olive-leaf-extract/research/).

Bottom line: **not “no,” but “insufficient/low-certainty evidence for a modest effect in mild hypertension.”** Anyone with high BP should not substitute olive leaf extract for prescribed treatment or clinician monitoring.
